title: Mercedes reveal how close Antonelli came to Mexico DNF
excerpt:
Mercedes have revealed that issues on Kimi Antonelli’s car in the late stages of the Mexico City Grand Prix nearly caused him to retire from the race, with the Italian clinging on until the chequered flag to be crowned World Champion.

In an ideal world for Antonelli, he needed to outscore his nearest title rivals George Russell and Lewis Hamilton by just two points at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez in order to clinch his maiden title, but he went above and beyond by finishing in third place.

However, he came close to not completing the race at all due to problems that were only revealed once it was over, leaving Deputy Team Principal Bradley Lord to declare that it was “a sign of the fact that this is Kimi’s year”.

Speaking on the High Performance Racing podcast, Lord explained: “We got the car back after the race, took the floor off the bottom – covered in oil!

“Sump cracked and Kimi said he thinks about four laps from the end he could start to feel the engine just starting to struggle, so [he was] right on the edge of retirement of that race and yet it held together.”

Following a bold overtake on Charles Leclerc to improve from P4 to the podium, the 20-year-old nursed his W17 to cross the line behind race winner Max Verstappen and Ferrari’s Hamilton.

That pass meant that the rostrum featured a magnificent 12 Drivers’ Championships in total, making for an emotional celebration between the trio.

Asked why Antonelli risked such a move on Leclerc, Lord said: “He's a racer and that was what was going to put him on the podium. Charles had had that massive lock-up at the restart. His tyre was down to the canvas.

“They were talking about boxing because of it, so Kimi saw an opportunity and it was, I think, the cleanest Turn 1 overtake we saw all day – on the brakes, ran him through the apex, and it was absolutely brilliant.

“That's one of the things Kimi has. Even in Singapore where Lewis and Lando [Norris] were sort of having their coming together, you just watch how he drives those four or five corners in Singapore to pick off two spaces against the reigning World Champion and the most successful driver the sport's ever seen battling with old and degrading tires.

"Kimi is utterly clinical when it comes to doing the bit that comes instinctively, and that's so impressive. Toto [Wolff] was cool. We realised what it brought about as well – suddenly you've got this podium of Max, Lewis, and Kimi.”

title: F1 champion Alan Jones passes away, aged 80
excerpt:
Formula 1 was today mourning the loss of Alan Jones, the Australian driver who claimed the 1980 Formula 1 World Championship with Williams.

Born on November 2 1946 in Melbourne, Australia, ‘Jonesy’ as he was known made his first F1 entrance at the 1975 Spanish Grand Prix with the Hesketh squad.

But while he would also race for Surtees, Beatrice Lola, Hill and the Shadow team – with whom he would claim his maiden victory, at the 1977 Austrian Grand Prix – it is with Williams that Jones is most associated.

A favourite driver of team boss Sir Frank Williams and technical chief Sir Patrick Head, Jones took the team’s first podium at Watkins Glen in 1978 and their first pole position at Silverstone in 1979.

He would go on to claim five victories out of 14 in the 1980 season, to become Australia’s second World Champion, after Sir Jack Brabham – while 11 of his 12 F1 victories would come with the team.

“Alan was the greatest fun, a terrific driver,” Head recalled in a 2012 interview.

“Alan was already a Grand Prix winner, and his arrival [at Williams] made us say, ‘We’d better shape up here’. It wasn’t as if we weren’t already working hard, but it gave us a focus that maybe we hadn’t had before.”

Jones would ultimately leave Formula 1 in 1986, going on to enjoy a second career as a broadcaster in his native Australia.

Paying tribute to Jones, Formula 1 President and CEO Stefano Domenicali said: “I am deeply saddened by the passing of Alan Jones, a true great of our sport and an extraordinary racer. Alan was a formidable competitor, a natural leader and an icon who inspired generations of fans, particularly in his beloved Australia.

“His place in Formula 1 history is assured, not least for bringing Williams their first Drivers’ and Constructors’ World Championships in 1980, a defining moment for the team and our sport. But beyond his achievements on track, Alan will be remembered for his character, his passion and the lasting mark he left on Formula 1.

“He will be greatly missed by the entire Formula 1 family. On behalf of Formula 1, I send my heartfelt condolences to his family and loved ones. Our thoughts are with them at this very sad time.”

BEYOND THE GRID: 1980 World Champion Alan Jones on racing and winning for Williams

A statement posted by the Williams team read: “Everyone at Williams is deeply saddened to learn of Alan Jones’ passing. Alan was instrumental in making Williams what it is today, forming an extraordinary bond with Frank Williams and Patrick Head to become our first Drivers' World Champion in just our fourth season in Formula 1.

“He set the standard for Williams champions: a fast, uncompromising racer with a challenger mentality who loved motor racing and dedicated his life to it. He is a true Australian icon and a Williams legend, and he will be dearly missed. We send our love and thoughts to the Jones family and all his friends.”

title: Where did it go wrong for Russell – and can he regroup for 2027?
excerpt:
The stadium at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez is a superb sporting stage. When it’s the scene of a champion's coronation the atmosphere becomes truly special – as we witnessed on Sunday for Kimi Antonelli.

title: When could Mercedes win the 2026 Teams' Championship?
excerpt:
Mercedes head to Brazil this weekend with a real possibility of sealing the Teams' Championship title. The Silver Arrows lead the standings by 126 points from Ferrari after a double points finish in Mexico City.

Kimi Antonelli has already wrapped up the Drivers' Championship, winning last weekend courtesy of his P3 finish at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez.

But what does his team have to do to win the other crown at Interlagos, or will the title fight rumble on to the final triple-header?

How many points are still up for grabs?

There are four rounds remaining in the 2026 season, so a maximum of 172 points remain up for grabs if a team records a 1-2 at every Grand Prix.

No team has got close to doing that this season, with Mercedes recording back-to-back 1-2 finishes in the first two rounds and again in Monza.

Ferrari have only had both drivers on the same rostrum once, at Silverstone.

Which teams are still in contention for the title?

Mercedes lead the way, with Ferrari the only team who can still catch them. Both Red Bull and McLaren have dropped out of the fight.

Mercedes have scored 630 points so far in 2026, with Antonelli taking nine Grand Prix wins and George Russell three.

Ferrari have ammassed 504 points, but they have only bagged two Grand Prix victories - one for Lewis Hamilton in Barcelona, and one for Charles Leclerc at Silverstone.

Despite Max Verstappen's late season form, winning three of the last four races, Red Bull are too far back and have already dropped out of contention.

Teams' standings after the Mexico City Grand Prix

When can Mercedes win the title?

Mercedes had a slim chance of winning both titles in Mexico City, but they needed an unlikely set of results to clinch the Teams' Championship last weekend.

However, in Brazil they have a bigger chance. If they leave Interlagos more than 128 points ahead of Ferrari, they will have done enough to take the title. There will be 129 points left on the table after this weekend, but given Mercedes have won more races, in the event of a tie they would win on countback.

With a lead of 126 points already, Mercedes do not need to do much to clinch the title next weekend. They simply need to outscore Ferrari by three points or more.

If Ferrari fail to score, an eighth-place finish for either Antonelli or Russell would be enough for Mercedes to seal the title, while a Ferrari 1-2 would guarantee the championship battle continues beyond Brazil.

If Ferrari win the race, Mercedes can still clinch the title if Antonelli and Russell finish high enough up the order, provided the other Ferrari finishes lower down.

Should Mercedes fail to secure the crown at Interlagos, their next opportunity will come at the Las Vegas Grand Prix, before the season concludes in Qatar and Abu Dhabi.

title: Camara concedes ‘there is a lot to learn’ ahead of F1 debut
excerpt:
Rafael Camara has admitted that “there is a lot to learn” as he prepares to drive a 2026 Formula 1 car for the first time at this weekend’s Sao Paulo Grand Prix, with the Brazilian replacing Esteban Ocon at Haas.

Reserve driver Ryo Hirakawa had been drafted into the American squad last time out in Mexico City, but with a World Endurance Championship finale to contest, he is to step aside for Camara to make his debut at his home event.

While Haas had previously confirmed that the Ferrari junior – who is currently leading the F2 standings – will race for them next season, they have brought his first race forward before he takes on the full-time driver role.

Addressing the opportunity, Camara said in the team's weekend preview: “I’m grateful to TGR Haas F1 Team for giving me this opportunity, and I also want to thank Ferrari for their continued support.

“Making my Formula 1 debut in Brazil is a special moment for me. I know there is a lot to learn, and my focus is on working closely with the team, understanding the car and doing the best job I can this weekend.”

Upon the news of Camara’s 2027 contract, Team Principal Ayao Komatsu explained that the 21-year-old had shown impressive pace during a two-day test in Haas’ 2025 challenger at Portimao, convincing him of the rookie’s speed and ability to handle pressure.

That prior experience will help to an extent when he competes alongside his new team mate and fellow Ferrari-backed driver Ollie Bearman, with the Briton hopeful to maximise Haas’ potential after frustrating back-to-back retirements in the United States and Mexico.

There’s also a sense of history repeating itself for Bearman as he similarly made a late appearance for the team at the Sao Paulo venue in 2024, albeit with multiple FP1 runs and two Grands Prix already under his belt.

“This triple header hasn’t been too kind to me so far, we’ve had promising pace, but I’m yet to cross a finish line,” he said. “I’ll be ending that streak this weekend in São Paulo, and what a track to have a great result on with the history and the fans – this city has it all.

“I’ve raced for the team here twice already, subbing in for Kevin [Magnussen] in 2024, so I know a little about how Rafa will be feeling. The focus is to work together to get some points for the team as we head into the business end of the season.”

title: Rosberg opens up on Hamilton relationship after retirement
excerpt:
Nico Rosberg and Lewis Hamilton shared one of the most intense and memorable rivalries in F1 history, so it’s perhaps not surprising that the German believes they still won’t “be best friends” a decade after the “crazy intense” 2016 season.

The pair had competed alongside one another since their karting days, but their relationship unravelled over four seasons as Mercedes team mates between 2013 and 2016, during which Hamilton won two titles and Rosberg clinched one.

Their tumultuous partnership in that final year produced multiple costly clashes, such as at the Austrian and Spanish Grands Prix, but Rosberg ultimately secured his sole Drivers’ Championship by five points over the Briton.

He went on to announce his shock retirement from the sport just five days after his triumph, opening the door for Valtteri Bottas to join the Silver Arrows for the 2017 season and beyond.

“I apologise to all the fans at the time who wanted to see that fight go on because it was a great battle between Lewis and I,” Rosberg shared on the latest episode of official podcast F1 Beyond The Grid. “I'd given it my all and achieved my dream, and to go out on a high is something really valuable for the rest of my life.

“In hindsight, it was the right decision thankfully – I didn't know at the time. It was scary. It was very scary, but it was right for me. I could not have got better. I was at the peak, I know that.

“For me, [another season] was going to be tough because I just threw everything at [2016] – more than everything, and it was crazy intense. It was not really realistic to keep up that level year in, year out.”

He explained that while Team Principal Toto Wolff accepted that his decision was “definitive”, Non-Executive Chairman and former World Champion Niki Lauda was “more on the angry side” due to the position it left Mercedes in.

“I was compromising their team, unfortunately,” Rosberg admitted. “They now have to find a replacement and there was nobody there initially. That's why I decided on telling them so quickly and announcing my retirement so quickly – it was only for the team.

The top 10 driver/team combination wins in F1 history

“I would have preferred to do one month celebrating and then after one month say, ‘Oh, by the way, I'm going to end it here.’

"That would have been much nicer, because the retirement almost became a bigger thing afterwards than my winning, actually. For me, that was not optimal, but it didn't matter.

“The most important thing was to reduce how much I'm compromising the team, and not make it even worse unnecessarily. I wanted to tell them immediately, as quickly as possible so that they could have time to replace and rebuild.”

Although he still mingles in the F1 world, primarily as a pundit, Rosberg has no regrets about his retirement from racing and remains satisfied that he was able to go out on the high of being crowned champion – even if Hamilton made it a challenge at the season finale.

Reflecting on that momentous day in Abu Dhabi, Rosberg said: “Of course, he’s always gracious in those moments.

“Just like I also congratulated him when he won the championship and told him that it was deserved, you know, and then he congratulated me as well. It was a hard one, though, because he didn't obey the team orders. He was bunching us up.

“It triggered the risk that the team would lose the race win because there's [Sebastian] Vettel and [Max] Verstappen coming up from behind, and it's very clear that he's driving slowly on purpose, very slowly.

“It’s understandable in the situation that you're not just going to hand it to me at that moment and you try and keep it in the grey area and keep playing the game.

“For me now, in hindsight, it’s amazing that he did that because it just became all the nicer. It was horrible in the moment.”

Asked whether his relationship with Hamilton improved after his retirement, he replied: “Of course. Anything will thaw after that. It's fine now, it’s neutral.”

He rejected a comparison of their situation to that of Ayrton Senna and Alain Prost following the latter’s sabbatical in 1992, adding: “Maybe not to that extent I think because they really became friends, in a weird way.

“We're just neutral and it's okay, it's nice. We will just not be best friends ever, you know?”

title: The 5 drivers most likely to qualify fastest in Brazil
excerpt:
Max Verstappen may have won three of the last four races, including wins in the Bahrain, Singapore and Mexico City Grand Prix, but he was not able to secure pole position in all three races as Qualifying continues to provide a varied list of winners in 2026.

Lewis Hamilton picked up his first pole of the season in Mexico ahead of George Russell and Charles Leclerc, but the race was won by Verstappen, who qualified fourth and started fifth after being handed a one-place grid penalty.

In total, six different drivers have taken pole over the last seven rounds, with only Verstappen being a repeat winner, in Sepang and Singapore.

There is a slightly different look to the betting markets for Qualifying in Brazil, with the Ferrari duo of Hamilton and Leclerc given a better chance of taking pole than winning the actual race, while the fifth driver in the market is different to the race odds, with oddsmakers preferring the chances of Russell over Lando Norris.

Our expert betting writers have looked at the Qualifying odds and assessed the chances of the leading contenders for pole at Interlagos.

Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

Verstappen has been favourite for pole at the last two races in the United States and Mexico City but qualified only second and fourth-fastest in those races.

That hasn't stopped bookmakers from putting him at the top of the market for Qualifying again this week, and he is the same price that he was to grab pole in Mexico at 6/4 (2.50, +150).

Verstappen now has more wins than poles this season, but while his 2024 Sao Paulo success came from an unpromising starting position of 17th, his 2019 and 2023 victories there were both achieved from pole.

Sao Paulo Grand Prix race betting guide

Kimi Antonelli (Mercedes)

Kimi Antonelli took pole at six of the first 10 races this season, but since then he has been the fastest qualifier once which was in Austin, Texas.

Bookmakers are not prepared to take any chances with the newly-crowned World Champion and have made him the second-favourite for pole in Brazil at 5/2 (3.50, +250).

The Italian ace already has experience of two Qualifying sessions at this track, and went second-fastest to Norris in both the Sprint and Grand Prix last season.

Charles Leclerc (Ferrari)

Ferrari took their first pole of the season in Mexico City through Hamilton and there is little between their drivers in the Qualifying betting this week with both on offer at 5/1 (6.0, +500).

Leclerc was close in Q3 last week, taking third place on the grid, which followed his second place finish in Qualifying in Singapore and a disappointing fourth in Austin, where he had gone fastest in Q2.

The Monegasque driver has never taken pole at this track but he has been competitive in Qualifying in recent years, taking second in 2023 and setting the third-fastest time last season.

The 5 drivers most likely to win in Brazil

Lewis Hamilton (Ferrari)

Hamilton increased his tally of career pole positions to 105 with his success in Mexico City, and he has been given the same odds as Leclerc to be fastest in Qualifying this week, having been available at bigger odds than his team mate to take pole at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez.

Hamilton first took pole at Interlagos back in 2012 for McLaren and has also qualified fastest there for Mercedes in 2016 and 2018, although he had a tough time in Qualifying at this track last season, failing to reach Q3 in both Sprint Qualifying where he was 11th and Grand Prix Qualifying where he was 13th.

George Russell (Mercedes)

Russell is only sixth in the Grand Prix betting markets for Interlagos but he is ahead of Norris in the betting market for Qualifying at 12/1 (13.0, +1200) to take his first pole since Azerbaijan.

He has been the fastest qualifier five times this season and pulled out a great Q3 lap to earn a front-row start in Mexico before having deployment issues on the first lap of the race.

title: What tyres will the teams have for the Sao Paulo Grand Prix?
excerpt:
The 2026 F1 season marches on this weekend with the Sao Paulo Grand Prix, held at the ever-entertaining Autodromo Jose Carlos Pace – and tyre suppliers Pirelli have confirmed the compounds that will be in use throughout the weekend.

For this year's event, the C3 has been selected as the hard compound, with the C4 as the medium and C5 as the soft. This marks a shift towards the softer end of the range compared to last season, when Pirelli offered the C2, C3 and C4 over what was a Sprint weekend.

Drivers will get two sets of the hard tyre (marked white), three sets of the medium tyre (marked yellow), and eight sets of the soft tyre (marked red), as well as access to the green intermediate tyre and the blue full wets, should they be required.

An extra set of softs is reserved for those who reach Q3 in Qualifying, while all drivers must use at least two different slick compounds during the race, providing the track is dry.

"The Brazilian circuit features several changes compared to last season," reads Pirelli's weekend preview. "During the year, resurfacing work was carried out on the section between Turns 3 and 5 and between Turns 8 and 9.

"These newly surfaced areas could alter grip levels and track evolution over the course of the weekend, particularly affecting tyre behaviour over longer runs. The three free practice sessions will provide an opportunity to assess track evolution and understand how the new surface influences degradation and wear.

"Twelve months ago, tyre degradation was one of the key technical factors in Sao Paulo. Although graining was less pronounced than initially expected, the C2 compound (used as the hard tyre that year) showed some tendency to slide, while the C3 and C4 displayed significant degradation, albeit still allowing competitive stints. The most effective strategy proved to be a two-stop race.

"In terms of tyre loads, Interlagos generates overall lateral forces that are broadly average, while combining several high-speed corners with long straights. The layout therefore does not place extreme demands on the tyres, with loads distributed fairly evenly between the front and rear axles.

"The numerous overtaking opportunities offered by the circuit’s flowing layout give teams a degree of strategic flexibility, but managing degradation traditionally remains the key factor in maximising race performance. Finding the right balance between single-lap pace and tyre management over longer stints will be one of the main objectives of the teams’ trackside work during the Brazilian weekend.

"It is also worth remembering that, because of the event’s position in the calendar, Interlagos is a circuit where rain and significant temperature fluctuations are often a factor. Intermediate and full wet tyres could therefore come into play in Brazil once again this year."

For more information about Pirelli’s F1 tyres, visit pirelli.com.

title: Latest F1 driver suffers Mexico City illness as Brazil media day absence confirmed
excerpt:
Lance Stroll will miss Thursday's media day at Interlagos, Aston Martin has confirmed, as the Canadian continues to recover from a viral infection picked up at last weekend's Mexico City Grand Prix.

Stroll finished the Mexico City round before symptoms emerged, and the team has opted to keep him away from paddock duties ahead of the São Paulo Grand Prix as a precaution.

Fernando Alonso will step in for his team-mate in the second drivers' press conference, taking on media duties alongside his usual commitments.

In a statement, Aston Martin confirmed the situation and gave an update on Stroll's condition.

"Lance will miss media day today as he continues to recover from a viral infection contracted in Mexico," the team said.

"He is recovering well, and we are confident he will return to the paddock on Friday."

The 28-year-old is not alone in having picked up illness around the long haul between the Mexican and Brazilian rounds, a stretch of the calendar that has previously caused fatigue and health issues for drivers and team personnel alike.

Kimi Antonelli and Valtteri Bottas both missed media day in Mexico City through illness, while Sergio Perez also became unwell on the opening day of track action and was ruled out of a fan event and his media commitments.

Aston Martin has given no indication that Stroll's participation in Friday's practice sessions is in doubt, with the team instead framing Thursday's absence as a straightforward precaution rather than a concern over his race weekend.

title: Charles Leclerc misses Sao Paulo GP start after birth of daughter
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc will not attend Thursday's media day ahead of the Sao Paulo Grand Prix, after the birth of his daughter, Bianca.

The Ferrari driver is travelling to Brazil today, having stayed behind to be present for the arrival of his first child with partner Alexandra.

Thursday's schedule at Interlagos typically includes the FIA press conference and a raft of team broadcast and sponsor commitments, all mandatory under the sporting regulations unless a dispensation is granted.

Leclerc was not included in Thursday's media schedule and is being replaced by Dino Beganovic in first practice, as part of the mandatory rule for a rookie to feature in four FP1 sessions across a season.

Missing such commitments without an approved excuse can normally result in a summons and financial penalty from the stewards, but a case like Leclerc's would be treated as a standard exemption rather than a breach.

It remains unclear whether the Monegasque will also miss any on-track running on Friday from second practice onwards, or whether he is simply prioritising travel time to arrive in Sao Paulo in good time for Friday afternoon.

Leclerc heads into the Brazilian round having finished fourth in Mexico City, where he was penalised for an opening lap clash with Lewis Hamilton.

The timing means Leclerc becomes a father for the first time towards the end of a hectic triple-header, with him still in the fight for second in the drivers' championship.

title: Nico Rosberg issues 'forever grateful' Max Verstappen message: '50-50 chance of a crash'
excerpt:
Nico Rosberg has revealed he feared a race-ending crash with Max Verstappen during the title-deciding 2016 Abu Dhabi Grand Prix, admitting he is "forever grateful" to the Dutchman for racing fairly when stuck behind him.

Rosberg needed only to finish in the top three at Yas Marina to clinch his maiden world championship, but Lewis Hamilton's late-race tactic of backing the field up towards Sebastian Vettel and Verstappen turned a straightforward afternoon into a nerve-shredding ordeal.

The German, then racing for Mercedes, found himself boxed in directly behind Verstappen's Red Bull with his title hopes suddenly hanging by a thread, as Hamilton's strategy of deliberately slowing the pack began to bite.

Speaking on the Beyond the Grid podcast, Rosberg described the moment his race engineer Tony Ross delivered the instruction that changed everything.

"Ah, horrible, horrible," began Rosberg, discussing Hamilton backing up the pack. "Yeah, he was unfolding his strategy, and it was working. It was working perfectly. He put me behind Max Verstappen with that strategy.

"I should never have been behind Max Verstappen, and suddenly I'm behind Max Verstappen, the worst guy to be behind. It was Mad Max at the time. It was a 50-50 chance of a crash if you ever tried to pass him or whatever. 50-50.

"So Lewis, it was working. His strategy was working. Yeah. And understandably, he has to do something. So he tries something, and it was working.

"And then probably the most extreme moment in my whole career is when Tony Ross, who I'm so grateful for because I have my whole career to kind of thank him for, I did every year except for one with him as my engineer, and there are many people to thank, but Tony Ross would be one, comes on the radio and says, 'Nico, your championship is at risk. You need to now pass Max Verstappen in the next two laps.'

"What? You don't pass Max Verstappen. Like, it's not something you do. Your championship is at risk. Like, what is that? Where does that come from?"

Nico Rosberg recalls suffering 'uncontrollable' foot shaking

Rosberg did find a way past, pulling off the overtake that effectively sealed the 2016 drivers' championship, with Verstappen eventually finishing fourth behind race winner Hamilton, Vettel and the German.

Nearly a decade on, Rosberg says the manner in which Verstappen defended still sticks with him, crediting the now four-time champion for racing him cleanly in one of the tensest moments of his career.

"Amazing move, and forever thankful to Max because he played it fairly, left the space," added Rosberg. "Forever grateful, like, amazing. Thank you so much, forever.

"And then I come out of that, and my next thought, I think you can start to realise that there was quite an intensity mentally going on here, so then I come out of that, and my foot starts shaking so much from fear and adrenaline that I'm uncontrollable on the throttle pedal.

"I'll never have that in my life again. I'll never experience that. I'd never had it before. The foot goes uncontrollable, jumping. The whole foot is jumping from adrenaline, from Max."

title: Charles Leclerc confirms Lewis Hamilton talks intention after 'grey area' exposed
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc taking to the grass on the opening lap in Mexico remains a big point of discussion.

Charles Leclerc has confirmed he intends to speak with Ferrari team-mate Lewis Hamilton after their opening-lap collision in Mexico City left Hamilton visibly frustrated and exposed what the Monegasque called a "grey area" in the rulebook.

The clash occurred on the first lap of the Mexico City Grand Prix, when Leclerc attempted an outside move on Hamilton into Turn 4. Both cars ran in deep and wide, with Leclerc cutting across the grass through Turn 5 to emerge in the lead. Hamilton rejoined the track before Turn 5 but lost the place to Max Verstappen in the process.

The stewards handed Leclerc a five-second time penalty for completing the overtake off-track and gaining a lasting advantage, reduced from the standard 10-second sanction because Hamilton had also run wide and the incident happened on the opening lap.

Ferrari served the penalty during Leclerc's scheduled pit stop rather than through an on-track swap, with Hamilton initially staying behind his team-mate having been beyond five seconds adrift.

Verstappen went on to win the race, with Hamilton second and Leclerc fourth behind Kimi Antonelli who clinched the title. A late red flag offered the seven-time champion a chance to attack.

Leclerc addressed the fallout with select media, including RacingNews365, after the chequered flag.

"We will talk about it, obviously," Leclerc said. "I don't know if he was very unhappy with what I did, because I felt like what he did was very much on the limit as well.

"I think he was maybe more angry with the whole situation, how the situation was dealt with in Turns 4 and 5 with the penalty, etc. So this is something we'll talk about for sure."

Leclerc's five-second punishment allowed him to build enough of a gap that the penalty carried little real consequence once served in the pits.

Pre-race notes had told drivers to give back positions before Turn 12 if they gained an advantage, yet cutting the corner let Leclerc pull clear in clean air.

Asked whether tougher penalties were needed for such scenarios, Leclerc did not shy away from the debate.

"Yeah, but there are also rules written down, and that's a difficult thing as well," Leclerc explained. "The thing is, if you take this situation by the rules, it's not so different from other situations.

"However, I do agree with you. Sometimes there are scenarios in which you gain more than the other, but, on paper, you've got to stick to the rules.

"So I think eventually we just need tracks that don't allow us to play with those kinds of limits and grey areas, because then it ends up being a bit of a difficult one. And I'm sure, yeah, many people will see it in a very bad way, which I understand, but it is what it is."

title: George Russell instructed to 'find an overdrive' or suffer 'game over'
excerpt:
George Russell must "find an overdrive" or face the prospect of it being "game over" in his partnership with new F1 drivers' champion Kimi Antonelli at Mercedes, according to Martin Brundle.

The former F1 driver highlighted what a critical juncture this is in the career of Russell, but nonetheless shared his belief that it will "make" and not "break" the Briton.

Heading into the season, the 28-year-old was the overwhelming favourite to clinch the drivers' title, his first. However, it quickly became evident that he was no match for his far less experienced team-mate, who took his first grand prix victory and followed that up with four more on the bounce, setting up an unexpected charge to his own maiden crown.

In doing so, Antonelli has become F1's youngest champion, the first Italian to win the title in 73 years, and only the third driver in contemporary Formula 1 to triumph in just his second campaign, after Jacques Villeneuve in 1997 and Lewis Hamilton in 2008.

It was anticipated that Russell would continue to have the measure of Antonelli, as he did through the 20-year-old's rookie year, but what was once an average advantage of around three-tenths in qualifying trim quickly evaporated.

"What will hit George hardest is that he couldn't match Antonelli for speed, for consistent speed, and that's all that matters in this business," Brundle told Sky Sports News.

"The stopwatch is a very antiquated system; despite spending hundreds of millions of dollars a year running two Formula 1 cars, we live and die by the stopwatch.

"And George has not been as fast as Kimi, especially in the second half of stints on a set of tyres. So that's what we'll get to George."

Brundle: 'There's an over in there somewhere'

Despite the devastation of losing a title that many in the F1 paddock had predicted would be his, Brundle believes Russell can use the experience to find a new gear and fight back next term.

"It might break George. I actually think it will make him. He'll find an overdrive. He's got to," the F1 driver-turned commentator added. "He's got to come back next year and just lift his game up if he's going to beat Kimi Antonelli.

"But I think meanwhile he's just had to suffer an awful season for himself, a brilliant season for a 19-year-old who then turned 20 through that season...

"George has either got an overdrive, or it's game over. There's an over in there somewhere."

title: Williams release statement after 'legend' Alan Jones saddening death
excerpt:
A heartfelt statement has been released by Williams.

Williams has paid tribute to Alan Jones following the death of its first world champion, who passed away on Wednesday at the age of 80.

Jones died three days after celebrating his 80th birthday, following a brief illness. His wife, Amanda, confirmed his death in a statement released through Motorsport Australia on behalf of the family.

The Australian won the 1980 Formula 1 world championship with Williams, the team's first drivers' title and the first of back-to-back titles for the Grove-based squad, which Jones delivered in just its fourth season competing in the sport.

Across a career spanning 117 race starts, Jones took 12 wins, 24 podiums and 206 points.

Williams released a statement reflecting on the impact Jones had on the team's early success, which read: "Everyone at Williams is deeply saddened to learn of Alan Jones' passing.

"Alan was instrumental in making Williams what it is today, forming an extraordinary bond with Frank Williams and Patrick Head to become our first drivers' world champion in just our fourth season in Formula 1. He set the standard for Williams champions: a fast, uncompromising racer with a challenger mentality who loved motor racing and dedicated his life to it.

"He is a true Australian icon and a Williams legend, and he will be dearly missed. We send our love and thoughts to the Jones family and all his friends."

After leaving Formula 1, Jones built an extensive career in sports car and touring car racing, winning the 1978 Can-Am Challenge Cup and finishing sixth overall at the 1984 24 Hours of Le Mans. He later became a fixture of Australian motorsport broadcasting and served the FIA as a driver steward at Grands Prix from 2010 onwards.

Driver

Alan Jones

Australian

F1 CEO 'deeply saddened' by tragic Alan Jones loss

The messages reacting to the tragic passing of Jones continued to roll in on Thursday morning, with F1 CEO and president Stefano Domenicali sharing his thoughts on the "deeply saddening" loss.

Domenicali's statement read: "I am deeply saddened by the passing of Alan Jones, a true great of our sport and an extraordinary racer. Alan was a formidable competitor, a natural leader and an icon who inspired generations of fans, particularly in his beloved Australia.

"His place in Formula 1 history is assured, not least for bringing Williams their first Drivers’ and Constructors’ World Championships in 1980, a defining moment for the team and our sport. But beyond his achievements on track, Alan will be remembered for his character, his passion and the lasting mark he left on Formula 1.

"He will be greatly missed by the entire Formula 1 family. On behalf of Formula 1, I send my heartfelt condolences to his family and loved ones. Our thoughts are with them at this very sad time."

title: F1 concern raised over 'two leagues' divide as latest rules change bites again
excerpt:
The new F1 regulations this year have created an obvious split in the competitive order.

Pierre Gasly has highlighted that F1 appears to be operating as "two leagues" due to the major gap that exists between the top four teams and the rest of the pack.

New regulations introduced this year have aided the spread, a situation that has been commonplace in F1 over the last handful of rule resets.

In 2025, the last year of the previous cycle of regulations, the competition was among the closest ever seen in the sport as the teams struggled to uncover additional pace.

Gasly is hopeful that a similar picture will be conjured in F1 in the coming years as the development peak reaches its limit.

"If you look at 2025, it was probably the most bunched-up field that we had," Gasly told media including RacingNews365.

"Looking at the past, every time you threw new regulations, they targeted bringing the field closer.

"I don't know if the stats back me up, but every time it feels like all the gaps get bigger and then eventually get smaller as the regulation and everybody gets to the maximum of what you can do.

"Let's give it another year or two, and hopefully that field can get quite close."

[Article continues below]

Driver

Pierre Gasly

French

10

Gasly calls on Alpine to do 'better job' amid performance gap

While a major gap exists in the standings between fourth and fifth, Gasly highlighted that the fight between the front-runners has been enjoyable to watch.

The Alpine driver insisted that it is up to the teams lagging behind to ensure they can catch up going forward.

"If I look at the top four, for motorsport fans, it's quite exciting at the moment.

"You had the McLaren winning, you had the Ferrari winning at some point. Red Bull and Max are back. Mercedes is very competitive.

"From that front, it's quite tight. It's just the gap between these top teams and the midfield, which is, at the moment too big, there is two leagues within the same league.

"At the end of the day, I don't want to complain about that because it's down to us to do a better job and deliver a better performance, and that's what we're going to focus on."

title: Audi take covers off striking Sao Paulo Grand Prix special livery
excerpt:
Audi has revealed a special livery for the São Paulo Grand Prix, designed by title partner Revolut to mark Gabriel Bortoleto's home race at Interlagos.

The design extends well beyond the car itself. Special race suits, pit crew suits and garage branding have all been produced to carry the same city-inspired theme across the team's entire race-weekend presence.

The launch builds on a wider campaign between Audi and its partners, following the earlier release of the Revolut 'São Paulo' Card and the adidas Sampa Soul collection. The livery reveal is being billed as the next step in a shared creative direction running across the team.

Central to the look is the Piso Paulista pattern, a geometric design taken from São Paulo's distinctive pavement. That same pattern links the livery to the race suits, the pit crew suits and the garage branding, tying together the cars, the drivers and the full team environment for the weekend.

Both Bortoleto and team-mate Nico Hülkenberg will wear race suits featuring the pattern at Interlagos. For Bortoleto, the Brazilian driver, the weekend carries extra weight as he races in front of his home fans for the first time this season.

Audi's chief brand and commercial officer, Stefano Battiston, explained the thinking behind the project.

"São Paulo has an unmistakable identity, and we wanted that to run through everything we bring to this race," Battiston said.

"Revolut's Audi R26 special livery takes the story onto the track, building on the Revolut card and the adidas Sampa Soul collection, with the race suits and garage branding completing that shared creative language.

"It shows what we can create when we bring our partners together: each contributes its own expertise, while the result feels connected. For Gabi's home race, that makes this a particularly meaningful expression of who we are as a team and how we connect with fans."

title: Kimi Antonelli heralded by F2 CEO after 'emotional' and universally popular F1 title win
excerpt:
When Kimi Antonelli took the chequered flag at the Mexico City Grand Prix, he became Formula 1's youngest drivers' champion.

And, at only 20 years of age (and 68 days), he didn't just beat Sebastian Vettel's 16-year-old record; he smashed it by over three years.

It's something Fernando Alonso and Lewis Hamilton once achieved, before Vettel etched his own name over theirs in the history books.

Remarkably, Max Verstappen — Formula 1's previous prodigy — could not reach such great heights so early in his career, despite making his F1 debut at 17.

It's almost impossible to imagine anyone being able to top Antonelli's incredible feat; they would almost certainly need to still be a teenager to do so.

So whatever happens over the rest of his career, as successful as he may become or otherwise, he will likely always have this one slice of F1 history, at the very least.

However, in winning the title, Antonelli has also achieved a thing so rare and elusive that Alonso, Hamilton, Vettel — and Verstappen — could only ever dream of.

It's something that the record books cannot measure nor recognise — not that it makes it any less significant...

For Antonelli has done something they — as divisive characters, as most sportspeople are — could never do. He is the universally popular champion.

And it is precisely that which makes this such a feel-good story for Bruno Michel, the man who oversaw Antonelli's single campaign in Formula 1's support paddock as he prepared to step into the greatest void left by Hamilton at Mercedes.

Speaking exclusively to RacingNews365, Michel touched upon the "mutual and common reaction" when sharing his own response to Antonelli's triumph.

"Number one, I think it's great news," the FIA Formula 2 and FIA Formula 3 CEO says. "It's great news for motor racing; it's great news for Formula 1.

"It's a big breath of fresh air, I would say, coming into the system, and it's really nice because Kimi is young and is also such a nice guy.

"It's really a pleasure to see that and to see how everybody's happy about it. And it's something that is completely a mutual and common reaction from everybody: the drivers, the team principals, the F1 people, us [Formula 2]. Everybody's happy. Of course, the Italians, obviously, but it's great.

"So, the first reaction is that we were all very, very happy to see him crowned after the race in Mexico, and the celebrations were quite emotional, I must say, and very, very nice. So, all good for F1 and all good for motor racing."

[Article continues below]

Michel echos FIA President and Vettel

Not only has Antonelli become the most popular F1 drivers' champion in living memory, but he is also the first Italian to do so in 73 years, which is frankly astounding given the passion for motorsport that envelops the country.

And after Juan Manuel Fangio, Jacques Villeneuve and Hamilton, he is one of just four people to be crowned in only their second season in the championship.

So momentous is his achievement that the only fear now is that success changes him from the genuine, warm character that has lit up the F1 paddock since his debut just 20 months — and 43 grands prix — ago.

It was something Mohammed Ben Sulayem requested in his congratulatory message to the newly crowned champion, about whom no one seems to have a bad word to say.

Asked if he had a message for Antonelli, Michel concurred with the FIA President, saying: "Well, what Mohammed said. I think, for me, it is important to see those drivers not changing.

"And we see that; it's very interesting in Formula 2, because some drivers, when they go from Formula 2 to Formula 1, they just disappear from our radars.

"And some others, they're always there. They come back. They come back on the pit wall. They see their old teams. They love to talk to them. It reminds them of good memories and stuff like that, and that's really what I would love to see with Kimi, even if he was with us not so long, but that he doesn't change."

Vettel, once a polarising figure in Formula 1 who has grown to be widely loved and adored, imparted some words of wisdom to Antonelli upon the young Italian surpassing his mark.

Michel underlined how valuable that message will be for the Mercedes driver as he reaches a higher plane.

"There was a very nice message that I heard from Sebastian Vettel that he sent to Kimi, saying being world champion is going to change the way people look at you, but make sure it doesn't change the way you look at people," he said.

"And to me, I think that's a very, very strong message. We've all been in this business for a long time. We know what can happen.

"I hope it keeps this freshness and this approach, which, of course, is going to be very difficult because now he's going to be under many, many more requests, and he's going to come into the paddock, and he's going to be the world champion. And we all know what it means.

"But if he can remain as close as possible to how he is now, then it will be a fantastic achievement as well."

title: Lewis Hamilton delivers 'way worse' verdict after Ferrari tension
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton was involved in an opening lap skirmish with team-mate Charles Leclerc at the Mexico City Grand Prix last weekend.

Lewis Hamilton has stated the intra-team tension was "way worse" at Mercedes compared to the current situation with Charles Leclerc at Ferrari.

The duo endured a tense Sunday in Mexico City last weekend after Leclerc attacked Hamilton for the lead of the race on the opening lap, with both drivers running off the circuit.

Hamilton admitted after the race that he was very annoyed over the situation, with Red Bull and Max Verstappen capitalising on the situation to take the victory.

Hamilton has endured strain with his team-mates in the past, including with Fernando Alonso at McLaren and Nico Rosberg at Mercedes.

The seven-time champion asserted the rivalry he had with Rosberg was far more torturous than his skirmish with Leclerc.

"I've had way worse times at Mercedes," Hamilton told media including RacingNews365.

"There were some really bad moments, but no, I don't really see there being huge differences.

"It was managed well at Mercedes, and I think Fred's doing his best. I think Fred came and spoke to me before the race, and I think he was nervous.

"He wants these two drivers to do well."

[Article continues below]

Driver

Lewis Hamilton

British

44

Hamilton brands Leclerc move 'unnecessary'

The off-track moment allowed Verstappen to slip ahead of Hamilton, and eventually move in front of Leclerc, who was handed a five-second time penalty for illegally gaining an advantage.

Hamilton doubled down that the move was "unnecessary" from Leclerc as Ferrari missed out on adding a third victory trophy to its cabinet this year.

"If I'm coming from behind and I'm taking all the risk and it ends up that we lose as a team, then I think I have some answering to do, because it impacts a lot of people," he said.

"But the other way around, I'm in the lead, and it was just unnecessary.

"I think we could have easily had that one-two today, which would have been huge for the team and for everyone back at the factory who's worked so hard to bring us these upgrades.

"I don't really know what will be done because up until now nothing really has been done. So, yeah, we'll see."

title: Alan Jones, 1980 F1 world champion, dies aged 80
excerpt:
Alan Jones, the 1980 Formula 1 world champion, has died, aged 80.

Jones, the last Australian to win the F1 title, passed away three days after celebrating his 80th birthday on Monday, after a battle with a short illness.

Jones is survived by his wife Amanda, with whom he shares twins Zara and Jack. He also has a daughter, Camilla, from a previous relationship, and an adopted son, Christian.

"We are extremely saddened to announce the passing of our beloved Alan, who passed away on 5 November following a short illness,” Amanda said in a statement issued to Motorsport Australia.

"He will be dearly missed and fondly remembered by those closest to him, as well as the many fans whose support he was always grateful for.

"Alan dedicated his life to motorsport, building a legacy that will live on through the countless people he touched along the way.”

"Through his achievements, passion and unmistakable character, both on and off the track, Alan left an enduring mark on the sport both nationally and across the globe.

"As a family, we would like to take this opportunity to thank everyone who was part of Alan’s journey for the many years of friendship, love and support. He was incredibly fortunate to have so many wonderful people around him."

Born in Melbourne on November 2nd, 1946, Jones made his F1 debut at the 1975 Spanish GP, before going onto take an stunning first career win for the unfancied Shadow team at the 1977 Austrian GP.

This performance, and a third place at that year's Italian GP, earned him a move to Williams for 1978, where he, Frank Williams, and Patrick Head were gaining momentum.

But it would not be until the 1979 German GP Jones won his first race for the team, being pipped to Williams' first win by one race as Clay Regazzoni took the honours at Silverstone.

A total of four wins in the final six races propelled him to third in the drivers' standings, but the Ferraris of Jody Scheckter and Gilles Villeneuve were too far ahead after their strong start.

But in 1980, Jones won four races and took five further podiums as he became the first Australian since Jack Brabham in 1966 to win the drivers' title - and took Williams' first title.

The team also won the constructors' - and defended it in 1981, but Jones could only finish third in his title defence as Nelson Piquet took the crown.

After winning the season-finale in Las Vegas, Jones stepped away from F1, only to be enticed back in 1983 for a one-off appearance before being tempted back full-time with the Haas team - no relation to the modern Haas operation.

His season-and-a-half was blighted by retirements, with a fourth and fifth his best results before hanging his helmet up for good following the 1986 Australian GP - days before his 40th birthday.

In total, from his 116 starts, Jones won 12 grands prix, took 24 podiums, six pole positions, and 13 fastest laps as well as the 1980 drivers' title.

In 1978, Jones also won the CAN-AM sportscar championship in a dominant season, with five wins, a second, and a third from the nine races he took part in.

After retiring, Jones moved into a broadcast career with Australian TV, sometimes working with motorcycle champion Barry Sheene.

In 1980, he received an MBE for services to motor racing.

Alan Jones, 1980 Formula 1 world champion. November 2nd, 1946-November 5th, 2026.

Everyone at RacingNews365 sends their thoughts to the family and friends of Alan Jones at this difficult time.

title: Liam Lawson handed lopsided Cadillac backing for F1 future
excerpt:
A significant majority of F1 fans believe Liam Lawson should be signed by Cadillac for the 2027 F1 campaign.

There is uncertainty around the driver line-ups at both Racing Bulls and Cadillac, with the former believed to be weighing up sticking with Lawson or promoting F2 star Nikola Tsolov.

At Cadillac, rumours have persisted that Bottas' drive for next year is not certain, despite joining on what was originally described as a multi-year contract.

A couple of suitors are believed to be in contention for a driver at Cadillac next year, prompting RacingNews365 to ask the fans about which direction the team should take.

A whopping 93 per cent of those who responded believe Lawson is the right pick for the American squad.

Others, including Bottas, Esteban Ocon, and Colton Herta, shared minimal votes in the poll.
